title: nth Roots of Complex Numbers
short: A nonzero number has n nth roots spread evenly around a circle.
trouble: Students find only one root, forgetting to add multiples of 2π/n.

blocks.html: De Moivre's theorem raises a number to a power by multiplying its angle. Running it backward finds roots, and reveals something surprising: every nonzero complex number has exactly $n$ different $n$th roots.

The $n$th roots of $r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$ are $$\sqrt[n]{r}\left(\cos\frac{\theta + 2\pi k}{n} + i\sin\frac{\theta + 2\pi k}{n}\right), \quad k = 0, 1, \ldots, n - 1.$$ They lie on a circle of radius $\sqrt[n]{r}$, spaced $\frac{2\pi}{n}$ apart.

Suppose $w = s(\cos\varphi + i\sin\varphi)$ and $w^n = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$. De Moivre says $s^n = r$, so $s = \sqrt[n]{r}$, and $n\varphi$ must point the same way as $\theta$: $n\varphi = \theta + 2\pi k$ for some whole number $k$. Dividing by $n$, each $k$ from $0$ to $n - 1$ gives a different angle; at $k = n$ you are back where you started, a full turn later.

blocks.title: Cube roots of 8
steps: $2(\cos 0 + i\sin 0) = 2$; $2\left(-\frac{1}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i\right) = -1 + i\sqrt{3}$; and its conjugate $-1 - i\sqrt{3}$.

blocks.title: Fourth roots of a negative
steps: $2\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{4} + i\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2}\,i$, and the others are its rotations by quarter turns.

blocks.html: Finding only one root, the one with $k = 0$. A cube root problem has three answers, a fourth root problem four. Add $\frac{2\pi}{n}$ to the angle again and again until you have $n$ roots evenly spaced around the circle.
